catalog_quote: 2.31. Accent placement. Accent in Southeastern Tepehuan is usually a combination of additional loudness and higher pitch. The two prosodies generally coincide, except in connected discourse, where the pitch of a syllable is further influenced by intonation patterns. ... All native Southeastern Tepehuan words are accented on one of the first two syllables of the stem, including reduplicated forms. Of these two syllables, it is the HEAVIER one that is accented. If, however, they are equally HEAVY, then the first syllable is accented. There are two degrees of HEAVINESS: (a) LIGHT, an open syllable with a short vowel; and (b) HEAVY, a closed syllable with a short vowel or a syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong. ... Notice that in both cases it is the first HEAVY syllable that is accented. Thus the only time that the second syllable is accented is when the first syllable is light. ... […
sweep_summary: Two items, both Elizabeth Willett's 'Reduplication and accent in Southeastern Tepehuan': the 1979 SIL-UND Work Paper (open access; downloaded via an Internet Archive copy because UND Commons serves a not reachable by automated download to scripted clients) was read in full and states, p. 52 §3.1, that all words are accented on the first or second syllable of the stem, the heavier of the two winning and ties going to the first, with a three-grade weight scale (CV < CVC < CVV(C)) -- an explicit statement of the weight rule that confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding (catalog source Willett 1991 grammar remains the the deciding source; the 1979 quote is a better deciding quotation for the weight criterion). The 1982 IJAL version (DOI 10.1086/465726) is paywalled (could not be reached by automated download publisher page, no archived copy at the Internet Archive, no OA copy in Crossref/OpenAlex; priority low since the 1979 text is the same paper. Extra: Reyes Taboada 2014 (COLMEX thesis, already held by the project) independently confirms 'se acentúa la primera sílaba pesada de izquierda a derecha' within a two-syllable window (pp. 180-181, 194). all look-ups were done by direct URL/API.

new_statements.quote: 3.1 All words are accented on the first or second syllable of the stem, including reduplicated stems. Of these two syllables, the one of heaviest grade is accented. If they are equally heavy, the first one receives the accent. There are three degrees of heaviness. An open syllable with a short vowel is the lightest. A closed short syllable resulting from final vowel dropping or from the suffixing of a consonant is heavier. A syllable with a vowel sequence is the heaviest.

new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive, bounded stress: a two-syllable window at the left edge of the stem; the heavier of the two syllables (CVV(C) > CVC > CV) is stressed, ties go to the first syllable. Stress is predictable from underlying vowel length. This is the explicit weight rule behind the catalog's 'weight' coding; Reyes Taboada 2014 (pp. 180-181, 194) independently confirms the same rule with instrumental data.

sources.citation: Willett, Elizabeth R. (1979). Reduplication and accent in Southeastern Tepehuan. Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session 23: 47-65 (Article 6). DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol23.06.
sources.quote: 3.1 All words are accented on the first or second syllable of the stem, including reduplicated stems. Of these two syllables, the one of heaviest grade is accented. If they are equally heavy, the first one receives the accent. There are three degrees of heaviness. An open syllable with a short vowel is the lightest. A closed short syllable resulting from final vowel dropping or from the suffixing of a consonant is heavier. A syllable with a vowel sequence is the heaviest. (p. 52) ... Accent always falls on the first or second syllable of a stem in native Tepehuan words. (fn. 2, p. 62)
sources.note: Stress (loudness + higher pitch, §3 p. 51) is predictable, not phonemic: within a two-syllable window at the left edge of the stem, the heavier syllable is stressed (three-way weight scale: CV < CVC < CVV(C)); ties go to the first syllable. Length, not accent, is underlying. Confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding and makes the weight criterion explicit where the catalog's 1991 quotation only gives the two-syllable window.

sources.quote: En tepehuano el acento es culminativo, ya que sólo hay un acento por palabra. También es delimitativo, pues se coloca lo más cerca posible del margen izquierdo de la raíz. Es sensible a la cantidad, pues se acentúa la primera sílaba pesada de izquierda a derecha (§5.1.2, p. 180) ... En el tepehuano del sureste se acentúa la primera sílaba pesada de izquierda a derecha. (§5.1.3, p. 181) ... no se encuentran palabras que lleven el acento más allá de la segunda sílaba. Por esta razón asumo que hay una ventana acentual (cf. Willet 1991) (§5.1.5, p. 194) [Translation: In Tepehuan accent is culminative, only one accent per word. It is also delimitative, placed as close as possible to the left edge of the root. It is quantity-sensitive: the first heavy syllable from left to right is accented ... no words carry accent beyond the second syllable, so I assume an accentual window.]
sources.note: Independent first-hand (instrumental) confirmation: vowel length is phonemic; stress falls on the first heavy syllable from the left, within a two-syllable window; duration is the main phonetic correlate, pitch and intensity secondary (§5.1.4). Confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding.
